html:
Polynesian voyagers reached New Zealand, Aotearoa, in the late 1200s and settled it in several canoe voyages. It was the last large land on Earth to be settled by people. Their descendants became the Māori.

The settlers came from eastern Polynesia, probably the Society and Cook Islands, at the end of the great wave of voyaging described in Settlement of East Polynesia. They sailed double hulled canoes, guided by stars, swells and birds. Dates come from radiocarbon, from rat gnawed seeds, and from early sites such as Wairau Bar, where tools and ornaments match those of the tropical islands. Māori tradition names the canoes of the first ancestors.

New Zealand was far cooler and larger than any island they knew. They brought the sweet potato, kūmara, which grew only in the north, and hunted seals and the giant flightless moa, which were soon gone; see Moa hunted to extinction. Over the next centuries a distinct Māori culture grew, with fortified hill villages and carved meeting houses. The first Europeans, under Abel Tasman, arrived in 1642.
